content: The document titled Recommendations and Guidance on Hepatitis C Virus Self-Testing (July 2021) provides an in-depth analysis of the cost-effectiveness of self-testing for hepatitis C virus (HCV). The study, authored by Josephine G. Walker, Philippa Easterbrook, Emmanuel Fajardo, Elena Ivanova, Muhammad S. Jamil, Cheryl Johnson, and others, was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) and is available under a Creative Commons license. This license allows for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution of the work, provided proper citation is given. The WHO does not endorse specific organizations, products, or services mentioned in the publication. The study highlights the global burden of HCV, with an estimated 58 million people infected in 2021, of whom only 26% were aware of their diagnosis. HCV self-testing (HCVST) is proposed as a strategy to improve access to testing and increase awareness of HCV status. Self-testing involves individuals collecting their own specimens, performing a rapid diagnostic test (RDT), and interpreting the results. This approach has been successfully implemented for HIV testing and is now being explored for HCV. The study models the cost per HCV diagnosis and cure using HCVST compared to traditional facility-based testing in four diverse settings: men who have sex with men (MSM) in China (1% HCV prevalence), men aged 40–49 in Georgia (23% prevalence), people who inject drugs (PWID) in Vietnam (60% prevalence), and PWID in Kenya (13% prevalence). The analysis uses a decision-tree model with a one-year time horizon, incorporating data from HCV and HIV testing programs, expert opinions, and program costs. Key findings include: 1. Increased Testing and Diagnosis: HCVST increased the total number of people tested by 62%, with 65% of self-test users linking to confirmatory testing. However, the cost per diagnosis and cure was higher with HCVST compared to standard testing. 2. Cost Variations by Setting: The cost per diagnosis without HCVST ranged from $35 in Vietnam to $361 in Kenya. With HCVST, the incremental cost per diagnosis was $104 in Vietnam, $163 in Georgia, $587 in Kenya, and $2,647 in China. These differences were driven by variations in HCV prevalence and testing costs. 3. Cost per Cure: The incremental cost per cure was lowest in Georgia ($1,418) and highest in China ($4,956), reflecting differences in treatment costs and prevalence. 4. Sensitivity Analysis: Factors such as the cost of self-tests, uptake rates, linkage to care, and test sensitivity significantly influenced the cost-effectiveness of HCVST. Reducing the cost of oral-fluid-based tests, increasing uptake, and improving linkage to care reduced the cost per diagnosis and cure. The study concludes that while HCVST is more expensive than standard testing, it increases the number of people diagnosed and linked to care, which is critical for achieving global HCV elimination targets by 2030. HCVST is particularly cost-effective in high-prevalence populations, such as PWID. Policymakers must consider the cost of HCV treatment, the prevalence of infection, and the feasibility of implementing self-testing in different populations when deciding on its adoption. The WHO is developing guidance on HCVST, informed by this cost-effectiveness analysis, usability studies, and assessments of values and preferences. The findings emphasize the importance of integrating HCVST into existing testing pathways to maximize its impact on diagnosis and treatment outcomes.
